title: Informal Conjecture (generalization of 1.3 to bounded clique number)
statement_text:
The result that triangle-free graphs of large chromatic number have holes of $
u$ consecutive lengths is also true for graphs with bounded clique number rather than just triangle-free graphs: for all integers $
u > 0$ and $k \geq 3$ there exists $n$ such that if $G$ has no clique of cardinality $k$ and has chromatic number at least $n$, then for some $t$, $G$ has a hole of length $t+i$ for $1 \leq i \leq 
u$.
context_text:
A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and an $\ell$-hole is a hole of length $\ell$ (number of edges). The main result of the paper is that for every integer $
u>0$ there exists $n$ such that every triangle-free graph with chromatic number at least $n$ has, for some $t$, holes of all lengths $t+1,\dots,t+
u$ ($
u$ consecutive lengths, the smallest possibly arbitrarily large). This contains the triangle-free cases of earlier results on Gyárfás's conjectures (long holes, long odd holes, holes of length a multiple of three). The authors conjecture the same for graphs with bounded clique number, but have made no progress in proving it. They mention that since submission they (with Chudnovsky and Spirkl) proved Gyárfás's long odd holes conjecture, and that, for all $k,s,t$, graphs with no $k$-clique and large enough chromatic number have a hole of length $s$ modulo $t$; these do not give consecutive lengths.

paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. IV. Consecutive holes

title: Conjecture 1.5
statement_text: Let $F$ be an infinite set of positive integers with bounded gaps. Then $F$ is constricting.
context_text:
A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and an $\ell$-hole is a hole of length $\ell$ (number of edges). A set $F$ of integers is $k$-constricting if there exists $n$ such that every graph with chromatic number at least $n$ contains either a clique with $k$ vertices or a hole with length in $F$, and constricting if it is $k$-constricting for every $k$. Every constricting set is infinite, since there are graphs of arbitrarily large chromatic number and girth. The main result of the paper is that for every integer $
u>0$ there exists $n$ such that every triangle-free graph with chromatic number at least $n$ has, for some $t$, holes of all lengths $t+1,\dots,t+
u$ ($
u$ consecutive lengths, the smallest possibly arbitrarily large). As a consequence, the authors prove that every infinite set of positive integers with bounded gaps is $3$-constricting, and they conjecture this extension to all $k$, presenting it as the counterpart of their conjecture that graphs with bounded clique number and large chromatic number have holes of $
u$ consecutive lengths.

title: Problem 1.6
statement_text: Is there an infinite set $F$ of positive integers such that $F$ is constricting and has density $0$?
context_text: A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and an $\ell$-hole is a hole of length $\ell$ (number of edges). A set $F$ of integers is $k$-constricting if there exists $n$ such that every graph with chromatic number at least $n$ contains either a clique with $k$ vertices or a hole with length in $F$, and constricting if it is $k$-constricting for every $k$. Every constricting set is infinite (graphs of large girth and chromatic number exist), and the authors conjecture that every infinite set with bounded gaps is constricting (they prove it is $3$-constricting). Not every infinite set is constricting, not even one of upper density one: take $G_1$ null and, for $i>1$, $G_i$ triangle-free with girth at least $2^{|V(G_{i-1})|}$ and chromatic number at least $i$; the set of cycle lengths occurring in no $G_i$ is not constricting. Lower density seems closer to the truth; the authors cannot rule out that a set is constricting if and only if it has positive lower density, although this does not seem likely. They conjecture the answer to this question is positive, and ask the even stronger question whether some constricting $F=\{f_1,f_2,\dots\}$ has $f_{i+1}-f_i\to\infty$; both questions would be very interesting even for $3$-constricting sets.
notes: PDF source — math appears cleanly readable; authors conjecture the answer is positive

title: Problem 1.7
statement_text: Is there an infinite set $F = \{f_1, f_2, \ldots\}$ of positive integers such that $F$ is constricting and $f_{i+1} - f_i \to \infty$ as $i \to \infty$?
context_text: This is a strengthening of Problem 1.6; an affirmative answer would show that a constricting set can have gaps tending to infinity. The authors note it would be very interesting to answer both Problems 1.6 and 1.7 even in the weaker case of 3-constricting sets.

title: Informal Question (on 2.1 for ℓ = 4)
statement_text: The following might be true when $\ell = 4$ (it is proved for all $\ell\ge5$): let $\varphi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a non-decreasing function; does there exist $n$ such that every $(2,\varphi)$-controlled triangle-free graph with chromatic number more than $n$ has a $4$-hole?
context_text: A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and an $\ell$-hole is a hole of length $\ell$ (number of edges). For a vertex $v$ and integer $\rho\ge0$, $N^\rho[v]$ is the set of vertices at distance at most $\rho$ from $v$, and $\chi^\rho(G)$ is the maximum over $v$ of $\chi(G[N^\rho[v]])$. For $\rho\ge1$ and a non-decreasing $\varphi:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, a graph $G$ is $(\rho,\varphi)$-controlled if $\chi(H)\le\varphi(\chi^\rho(H))$ for every induced subgraph $H$ of $G$; roughly, every induced subgraph of large chromatic number has a vertex whose radius-$\rho$ ball has large chromatic number. In a triangle-free graph $\chi^1\le2$, so the radius-$2$ case is the first nontrivial one. The authors prove that for every non-decreasing $\varphi$ and every $\ell\ge5$ there exists $n$ such that every $(2,\varphi)$-controlled triangle-free graph with chromatic number more than $n$ has an $\ell$-hole (this is one of three steps of their proof that triangle-free graphs of large chromatic number have holes of $\nu$ consecutive lengths). They remark that it might be true for $\ell=4$ as well, but they have not been able to decide this.
notes: PDF source — phrased by authors as 'might be true … but we have not been able to decide this'; no formal conjecture label
